Taj Mahal.history: Built between 1631 and 1653 by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan as a mausoleum for his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal, the Taj Mahal is widely considered the finest example of Mughal architecture and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its white marble dome and intricate inlay work attract millions of visitors annually, making it a symbol of eternal love and India's most iconic monument.
Taj Mahal.fun_fact: The Taj Mahal's minarets are slightly tilted outward so that in the event of an earthquake, they fall away from the main tomb.

Humayun's Tomb.history: Completed in 1572, Humayun's Tomb was built by Hamida Banu Begum, wife of the second Mughal emperor Humayun. It was the first garden-tomb in the Indian subcontinent and a precursor to the Taj Mahal, blending Persian and Indian architectural elements. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and served as a model for later Mughal mausoleums.
Humayun's Tomb.fun_fact: Over 150 Mughal family members are buried within this complex, earning it the nickname 'Dormitory of the Mughals'.

Red Fort.history: The Red Fort (Lal Qila) was the main residence of the Mughal emperors for nearly 200 years, constructed between 1638 and 1648 by Emperor Shah Jahan when he moved the capital from Agra to Delhi. Its massive red sandstone walls enclose a complex of palaces, gardens, and museums. India's Prime Minister hoists the national flag here every Independence Day.
Red Fort.fun_fact: The fort was designed by architects Ustad Ahmad Lahauri and Hamid, the same team that built the Taj Mahal.

Agra Fort.history: Agra Fort is a UNESCO World Heritage Site that served as the main residence of the Mughal emperors until 1638. Originally constructed in 1565 by Akbar, it was later enhanced by Jahangir and Shah Jahan who added the white marble palaces. Shah Jahan was kept imprisoned here by his son Aurangzeb in his final years, with a view of the Taj Mahal across the river.
Agra Fort.built_by: Akbar (original), expanded by Jahangir and Shah Jahan
Agra Fort.fun_fact: Shah Jahan spent the last 8 years of his life imprisoned in Agra Fort, gazing at the Taj Mahal built for his wife.

Fatehpur Sikri.history: Built by Emperor Akbar in the 1570s as his new imperial capital, Fatehpur Sikri was abandoned just 14 years after completion, likely due to water scarcity. The city is a stunning blend of Hindu, Islamic, and Jain architectural styles, reflecting Akbar's inclusive philosophy. The Buland Darwaza, built to commemorate his victory over Gujarat, is one of the world's tallest gateways.
Fatehpur Sikri.fun_fact: The ghost city of Fatehpur Sikri was abandoned after only 14 years, yet its structures remain remarkably intact over 400 years later.

Itmad-ud-Daulah.history: Often called the 'Baby Taj', Itmad-ud-Daulah is a Mughal mausoleum built between 1622 and 1628 by Empress Nur Jahan for her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg, who served as chief minister to Emperor Jahangir. It is notable as the first Mughal structure entirely built of marble and the first to use pietra dura (gemstone inlay), a technique later perfected in the Taj Mahal.
Itmad-ud-Daulah.fun_fact: Known as the 'jewel box in marble', this was the first Mughal building to use white marble throughout and pioneered the gemstone inlay technique.

Jama Masjid Delhi.history: Built by Shah Jahan between 1644 and 1656, the Jama Masjid is the largest and most magnificent mosque in India, capable of accommodating 25,000 worshippers. Constructed using red sandstone and white marble, it stands on a 10-meter high platform and features three great gateways and four towers. It took 12 years and 5,000 workers to complete.
Jama Masjid Delhi.fun_fact: The Jama Masjid houses sacred relics of the Prophet Muhammad including a hair strand, sandal, and a footprint preserved in a marble block.

Qutub Minar.history: The Qutub Minar is a 72.5-metre tall minaret begun by Qutb ud-Din Aibak in 1193 and completed by his successor Iltutmish, making it a pre-Mughal Indo-Islamic monument. However, it was significantly restored and expanded during the Mughal period, particularly under Firuz Shah Tughlaq. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the tallest brick minaret in the world.
Qutub Minar.built_by: Qutb ud-Din Aibak (founded), restored by Mughals
Qutub Minar.fun_fact: The Qutub Minar is slightly tilted, leaning at approximately 65 cm from the vertical at the top, but is structurally stable.

Bibi Ka Maqbara.history: Built between 1651 and 1661 by Prince Azam Shah in memory of his mother Dilras Banu Begum, the first wife of Emperor Aurangzeb, Bibi Ka Maqbara is often called the 'Taj of the Deccan' due to its striking resemblance to the Taj Mahal. Despite a limited budget and local materials, the architects created a remarkable homage to its northern counterpart.
Bibi Ka Maqbara.fun_fact: Aurangzeb reportedly disapproved of the extravagant construction of this tomb for his wife, believing it wasteful of state resources.

Akbar's Tomb.history: The magnificent mausoleum of Mughal Emperor Akbar the Great is located in Sikandra near Agra, and was begun by Akbar himself in 1605 and completed by his son Jahangir in 1613. It uniquely blends Buddhist, Hindu, Islamic, Jain, and Christian motifs — a reflection of Akbar's syncretic religious philosophy known as Din-i-Ilahi.
Akbar's Tomb.fun_fact: Akbar personally oversaw the early construction of his own tomb, blending five different religious architectural styles to represent his syncretic beliefs.

Lahore Fort.history: Lahore Fort (Shahi Qila) is a citadel that has been rebuilt and expanded by successive Mughal emperors from Akbar to Aurangzeb. Akbar first built the current structure in 1566, while Shah Jahan added the iconic Sheesh Mahal (Palace of Mirrors) and the stunning Naulakha pavilion. The fort is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and testifies to the artistic brilliance of the Mughal era.
Lahore Fort.fun_fact: The Sheesh Mahal (Hall of Mirrors) inside Lahore Fort is decorated with thousands of tiny mirrors so that a single candle illuminates the entire room.

Badshahi Mosque.history: Commissioned by Emperor Aurangzeb in 1671 and completed in 1673, the Badshahi Mosque was the world's largest mosque for over 300 years until the 1980s. Its grand red sandstone courtyard can accommodate 55,000 worshippers. The mosque showcases the zenith of Mughal religious architecture with its white marble domes and exquisite stone carvings.
Badshahi Mosque.fun_fact: The Badshahi Mosque's courtyard is so large it can hold 55,000 worshippers, making it one of the world's largest mosque courtyards.

Shalimar Bagh.history: Shalimar Bagh (Garden of Love) was laid out in 1619 by Emperor Jahangir for his wife Empress Nur Jahan on the shores of Dal Lake in Kashmir. It is the finest example of a Mughal pleasure garden, divided into four terraced sections with fountains, water channels, and pavilions shaded by ancient chinar trees, representing the concept of Paradise on Earth.
Shalimar Bagh.fun_fact: The Shalimar Bagh contains a 400-year-old chinar tree planted during Jehangir's reign — a living witness to the golden age of Mughal Kashmir.

Moti Masjid Agra.history: The Pearl Mosque (Moti Masjid) inside Agra Fort was built by Shah Jahan between 1647 and 1654 for his personal use and that of the royal household. Constructed entirely of white marble with a glistening surface, it is celebrated as one of the most beautiful mosques in India, featuring three marble domes, graceful arches, and elegant calligraphy throughout.
Moti Masjid Agra.opening_hours: Part of Agra Fort timings (6:00 AM – 6:00 PM)
Moti Masjid Agra.fun_fact: The 'Pearl Mosque' earns its name from its lustrous, white marble surfaces that glow ethereally in moonlight, like a luminous pearl.

Safdarjung Tomb.history: Built in 1754, the Safdarjung Tomb is considered the last grand garden-tomb in the Mughal tradition, constructed for Safdarjung, the Prime Minister of Mughal Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur. Though built in a declining era of the Mughal empire, it still reflects the grandeur of the style with its red and buff sandstone, marble inlay work, and ornamental gardens.
Safdarjung Tomb.fun_fact: Safdarjung's Tomb is said to be the last monumental example of Mughal architecture built in India, marking the sunset of a great imperial tradition.
